title: Highly Available Control Plane
summary: Stacked vs external etcd, the API server load balancer, and building an HA control plane with kubeadm.

blocks.text: A busy port runs several harbor offices, each with its own front desk, load planner and supervisors, and ships reach them through a traffic marshal (load balancer). The question is where the master ledger (`etcd`) lives. **Stacked**: each office keeps its own copy and consults only that one; simpler, but losing an office loses a copy too. **External**: copies live in separate records buildings serving every office; sturdier, but twice the buildings. `kubeadm` stacks by default.

In both topologies every control plane node runs kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager, and worker nodes reach the API servers through a **load balancer**. The difference is where etcd lives.

rows: A local member on each control plane node
Each etcd member serves only its own node's kube-apiserver
Each etcd host talks to every control plane node's kube-apiserver
Simpler to set up and to manage replication
Losing one node hurts redundancy less
Losing a node loses a control plane instance **and** an etcd member

items: Stacked is the **kubeadm default**. `kubeadm init` and `kubeadm join --control-plane` create the local etcd member automatically.
Add more control plane nodes to reduce the coupled-failure risk of a stacked setup.

sections.heading: Load balancer for kube-apiserver
sections.sourceTitle: Creating Highly Available Clusters with kubeadm

blocks.text: The traffic marshal (load balancer) needs a name in the city directory (DNS), not just a bare address. It forwards callers to every healthy office, checking each by knocking on the front-desk door, port **6443**. Its address must always match the office address in the crew's plans (`ControlPlaneEndpoint`). Test before opening: "connection refused" is fine while no office exists yet, but a timeout means the marshal can't reach the office.

items: Give the load balancer a name that resolves in DNS. In a cloud, avoid pointing at a raw IP address.
Use a TCP forwarding load balancer that sends traffic to all healthy control plane nodes. The health check is a TCP check on the API server port (default **6443**).
The load balancer address must always match kubeadm's **ControlPlaneEndpoint**.
Add the first control plane node, test, then add the rest to the target group.

blocks.text: Before init, **connection refused** is expected (no API server yet). A **timeout** means the load balancer cannot reach the node, so fix its configuration.

sections.heading: Initialise the first control plane node
sections.sourceTitle: Creating Highly Available Clusters with kubeadm

blocks.text: Building the first office, the crew paints the marshal's address on it (`--control-plane-endpoint`) and, with `--upload-certs`, locks the shared office seals (certificates) in an encrypted strongbox, the **kubeadm-certs** Secret. The strongbox and its key expire after two hours; a joined office can re-upload them for a fresh key. That key unlocks sensitive port data, so keep it secret. Save the join slips and build the roads (CNI) before more offices join.

items: `--control-plane-endpoint`: the load balancer's address or DNS name and port.
`--upload-certs`: encrypts the certificates shared by all control plane nodes and stores them in the **kubeadm-certs** Secret.
The kubeadm-certs Secret and its decryption key **expire after two hours**. Re-upload and get a fresh key with `sudo kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs` on a joined control plane node.
`kubeadm certs certificate-key` generates a key you can pass with `--certificate-key` at init.
`--config` and `--certificate-key` can't be combined on init. With a config file, set the `certificateKey` field instead.
Save the printed join commands, then install a CNI plugin before joining further nodes.

blocks.text: The certificate key unlocks sensitive cluster data. Keep it secret.

sections.heading: Join more control plane nodes and workers
sections.sourceTitle: Creating Highly Available Clusters with kubeadm

blocks.text: Extra offices join with the same slip as ships, plus two extras: `--control-plane` ("I'm an office, not a cargo ship") and `--certificate-key`, which opens the strongbox and fetches the shared seals. Offices join one at a time, after the first is fully up. The phone directory staff (CoreDNS Pods) usually all crowd into the first office, so once another joins, spread them out with a `rollout restart`.

# extra control plane node
sudo kubeadm join <LB>:<PORT> --token <token> \
  --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash> \
  --control-plane --certificate-key <key>

# worker node
sudo kubeadm join <LB>:<PORT> --token <token> \
  --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash>

items: `--control-plane` makes the joining node a new control plane instance.
`--certificate-key` downloads the certificates from the kubeadm-certs Secret and decrypts them.
Join control plane nodes one at a time, after the first node is fully initialised.
CoreDNS Pods usually all land on the first node. After another node joins, spread them with `kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deployment coredns`.

blocks.text: Spot the difference fast: the control plane join command is the worker join command plus `--control-plane --certificate-key <key>`.

sections.heading: External etcd setup
sections.sourceTitle: Creating Highly Available Clusters with kubeadm

blocks.text: For separate records buildings (external `etcd`), build them first. Then carry their seals, the ledger CA plus the front desk's ledger client certificate and key, over to the first office, and write a plan (a kubeadm config file) listing the three ledger addresses and where those seals sit. Run `kubeadm init --config` with `--upload-certs`, and the remaining offices join exactly as in the stacked layout.

Set up the etcd cluster first. Then copy `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt`, `/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.crt` and `apiserver-etcd-client.key` from an etcd node to the first control plane node, and describe etcd in a kubeadm config file:

apiVersion: kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta4
kind: ClusterConfiguration
kubernetesVersion: stable
controlPlaneEndpoint: "LOAD_BALANCER_DNS:LOAD_BALANCER_PORT"
etcd:
  external:
    endpoints:
      - https://ETCD_0_IP:2379
      - https://ETCD_1_IP:2379
      - https://ETCD_2_IP:2379
    caFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt
    certFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.crt
    keyFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.key
Remaining control plane nodes join exactly as in the stacked case.

sections.heading: Sizing, quorum and manual certificates
sections.sourceTitle: Creating Highly Available Clusters with kubeadm

blocks.text: Run three or more offices, ideally an odd number, so choosing a lead office still works when a machine or district fails. Separate records buildings need three or more members too, an odd number for a clean vote (quorum). Copying seals by hand without the strongbox? Take only the short list of authority seals and keys; copying every certificate can break joins. These plans don't cover city-built public entrances or on-demand warehouse units.

items: Use **three or more** control plane machines. An **odd number** helps leader selection if a machine or zone fails.
External etcd needs three or more extra machines. An odd number of etcd members is required for optimal voting quorum.

Without `--upload-certs`, copy only these from the first node: `ca.crt`, `ca.key`, `sa.key`, `sa.pub`, `front-proxy-ca.crt`, `front-proxy-ca.key`, `etcd/ca.crt` and (stacked only) `etcd/ca.key`. Copying every certificate can break joins because of missing SANs.

blocks.text: This guide doesn't cover cloud providers: neither approach works there with LoadBalancer Services or dynamic PersistentVolumes.

questions.stem: Which topology runs an etcd member on every control plane node?

options.explanation: etcd is colocated with the control plane in the stacked topology.
External etcd runs on separate hosts.
That is not one of the two HA topologies.

questions.stem: You must survive a node loss with as little redundancy impact as possible and have hosts to spare. Which topology fits?

options.explanation: Decoupling etcd from the control plane limits the impact of losing one host.
Stacked loses an etcd member and a control plane instance together, and the page asks for at least three.
One node is not highly available.

questions.stem: True or false: The external etcd topology needs at least six hosts for the control plane and etcd together.

options.explanation: Correct: three control plane hosts plus three etcd hosts.
The page states a minimum of three of each.

questions.stem: Which command initialises the first node of a stacked HA control plane?

options.explanation: The endpoint points at the load balancer; --upload-certs shares the certificates.
That joins additional control plane nodes.
That re-uploads certificates on an existing control plane node.
This sets a Pod CIDR but gives no shared endpoint for HA.

questions.stem: Three hours after `kubeadm init --upload-certs`, joining a control plane node with the saved `--certificate-key` fails. Why, and what fixes it?

options.text: The kubeadm-certs Secret and key expired after two hours; run kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs and use the new key
options.explanation: Uploaded certs are deleted after two hours; re-uploading prints a new key.

options.text: The bootstrap token is missing; run kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deployment coredns
options.explanation: Restarting CoreDNS has nothing to do with certificates.

options.text: The load balancer must be removed; join directly to the first node IP
options.explanation: Control plane nodes should be reached via the load balancer endpoint.

options.text: etcd must be restored from a snapshot
options.explanation: Nothing is wrong with etcd.

questions.stem: Which flags must you add to a worker `kubeadm join` command to join a node as an extra control plane node (certs uploaded at init)? Select 2.

options.explanation: It tells kubeadm join to create a new control plane instance.
It decrypts the certificates from the kubeadm-certs Secret.
That is used with kubeadm init (or its upload-certs phase), not join.
That is an init flag for the Pod network.

options.text: Expected: the API server isn't running yet
options.explanation: The guide says connection refused is expected at this point.

options.text: The load balancer cannot reach the control plane node
options.explanation: A timeout would indicate that.

options.text: Port 6443 is blocked by a firewall on the client
options.explanation: The page treats refused as the normal pre-init result.

questions.stem: True or false: When using a kubeadm config file on init, you can still pass `--certificate-key` on the command line.

options.explanation: They cannot be mixed.
Correct. Put certificateKey in the config file instead.

questions.stem: For an external etcd cluster, where do you tell kubeadm the etcd endpoints?

options.text: In ClusterConfiguration under etcd.external.endpoints, with caFile, certFile and keyFile
options.explanation: External etcd requires a config file with these fields.
That is the API server load balancer endpoint.
Automatic management only applies to stacked etcd.
That decrypts uploaded control plane certificates.

questions.stem: You chose not to use `--upload-certs`. Which files do you copy from the first control plane node to the others? Select 3.

options.explanation: Cluster CA files are in the copy list.
Service account key pair is in the list.
Front proxy CA files are in the list.
Copying all certs can make joins fail due to missing SANs.

questions.stem: Why does the guide favour an odd number of control plane nodes?

options.text: It helps leader selection after a machine or zone failure
options.explanation: Stated in the prerequisites.

options.text: kubeadm refuses to join an even number
options.explanation: No such restriction is described.

options.text: The load balancer needs an odd target count
options.explanation: The load balancer has no such need.

questions.stem: After joining two more control plane nodes, all CoreDNS Pods still run on the first node. What does the guide suggest?

options.text: kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deployment coredns
options.explanation: Restarting the Deployment lets the Pods spread to the new nodes.
This only watches Pods.
This re-uploads certificates.

questions.stem: True or false: In the stacked topology, each etcd member talks to the kube-apiserver of every control plane node.

options.explanation: That describes external etcd.
Correct. A stacked etcd member talks only to its own node's kube-apiserver.
